questions.question: A bar model is divided into 10 equal parts. 4 of the parts are shaded green and the other 6 parts are left white. Which ratio compares the shaded parts with the WHOLE bar?
questions.explain: A part-to-whole ratio compares one part with every equal part in the bar, so shaded to whole is 4 : 10. The usual trap is answering 4 : 6, which is the part-to-part ratio (green to white), not a comparison with the whole.

questions.question: A bar model is divided into 12 equal parts. 5 parts are shaded blue and 7 parts are left white. Which ratio compares the shaded parts with the UNSHADED parts?
questions.explain: Shaded to unshaded is a part-to-part ratio, so it compares 5 blue parts with 7 white parts: 5 : 7. The trap is using 12, the whole bar, as the second number — that would make it a part-to-whole ratio instead.

questions.question: A bar model is divided into 9 equal parts. 2 parts are shaded orange and the other 7 parts are shaded purple. For this bar, what does the ratio 2 : 9 tell you?
options: There are 2 orange parts for every 9 purple parts.
The orange parts compared with the purple parts.
The orange parts compared with the whole bar.
The purple parts compared with the whole bar.
questions.explain: The number 9 is the total number of equal parts, so 2 : 9 compares orange with the whole bar — a part-to-whole ratio. The orange-to-purple comparison would be 2 : 7, because 7 is a part, not the whole.

questions.question: A bar model is divided into 6 equal parts, and exactly 1 part is shaded. Which statement about this bar is TRUE?
options: The ratio of shaded parts to the whole bar is 1 : 5.
The ratio of shaded parts to unshaded parts is 1 : 6.
Both the shaded-to-unshaded ratio and the shaded-to-whole ratio are 1 : 6.
The ratio of shaded parts to unshaded parts is 1 : 5, and the ratio of shaded parts to the whole bar is 1 : 6.
questions.explain: There are 5 unshaded parts, so shaded to unshaded is 1 : 5 (part-to-part), while shaded to the whole bar is 1 : 6 (part-to-whole). The common trap is thinking one ratio describes both comparisons — the second number changes depending on whether you compare with a part or with the whole.

questions.question: In a bag of counters, the ratio of red counters to yellow counters is 3 : 4. What is the ratio of red counters to the TOTAL number of counters?
questions.explain: Add the parts to find the whole: 3 + 4 = 7 counters in all, so red to total is 3 : 7. The trap is repeating 3 : 4, which only compares red with yellow and never mentions the total.

questions.question: At a pet store, the ratio of cats to ALL the pets is 2 : 9. What is the ratio of cats to the pets that are not cats?
questions.explain: Since 9 is the whole, the pets that are not cats make up 9 − 2 = 7 parts, so cats to non-cats is 2 : 7. The trap is reusing 9, but 9 counts the cats too, so it cannot be the other part.

questions.question: In a tile pattern, the ratio of blue tiles to green tiles is 5 : 3. Which of these is a correct part-to-whole ratio for the blue tiles in this pattern?
questions.explain: The whole is 5 + 3 = 8 parts, so blue to whole is 5 : 8, and doubling gives the equivalent ratio 10 : 16. The trap is doubling the part-to-part ratio into 10 : 6, which still compares blue with green, not with the whole pattern.

questions.question: In a Grade 6 class of 28 students, the ratio of students who walk to school to students who ride the bus is 2 : 5. Which ratio compares the walkers with the WHOLE class?
questions.explain: The 7 parts (2 + 5) share 28 students, so each part is 4 students and 8 students walk; walkers to the whole class is 8 : 28. The trap is 8 : 20, which is just the part-to-part ratio walkers-to-bus-riders written with the real numbers.

questions.question: Maya has 3 red apples and 2 green apples in her lunch bag. She says, “The ratio of red to green is 3 : 2, so red apples are 3/2 of my apples.” What is wrong with Maya's thinking?
options: She used the part-to-part ratio 3 : 2 as if it were part-to-whole; red is 3 out of 5 apples, so 3/5.
She flipped the fraction; the smaller number goes on top, so red apples are 2/3 of her apples, not 3/2.
She should have compared green with red, so the ratio is 2 : 3; a ratio always lists the smaller group first.
Nothing is wrong — 3 : 2 does mean 3/2 of the apples are red, since any ratio can be written as a fraction.
questions.explain: A fraction of the apples must compare a part with the whole, and the whole is 3 + 2 = 5 apples, so red apples are 3/5. The trap is turning a part-to-part ratio straight into a fraction, which would say she has more red apples than apples altogether.

questions.question: A trail mix recipe uses dried cranberries and almonds in the ratio 2 : 3. Jordan makes 250 g of trail mix for a hike at Golden Ears. How many grams of cranberries are in the mix, and why?
options: About 167 g, because cranberries are 2/3 of the mix.
100 g, because cranberries are 2 of the 5 equal parts of the whole mix.
125 g, because there are 2 ingredients, so the mix splits in half.
150 g, because cranberries are 3 of the 5 equal parts.
questions.explain: The ratio 2 : 3 is part-to-part, so the whole is 5 parts: 250 g ÷ 5 = 50 g per part, and cranberries take 2 parts, or 100 g. The trap is reading 2 : 3 as 2/3 of the mix — the 3 is the almond part, not the whole.

questions.question: At a Richmond hockey practice, 7 out of every 12 players wear a blue jersey and the rest wear white. Nadia says, “So the ratio of blue jerseys to white jerseys is 7 : 12.” Which correction is right?
options: The ratio of blue to white is 7 : 12, because 7 out of 12 players wear blue, so Nadia is right.
The ratio of blue to white is 12 : 7, because the bigger number in a ratio always goes first.
The ratio of blue to white is 7 : 5, because 12 is the whole team, not the white group.
The ratio of blue to white is 5 : 12, because 12 − 7 = 5 players wear white out of the 12.
questions.explain: Out of every 12 players, 12 − 7 = 5 wear white, so blue to white is 7 : 5, while 7 : 12 compares blue with the whole team. The trap is keeping the total as the second number when the question asks you to compare one part with another part.

questions.question: In Ms. Chen's class, the ratio of students who bike to school to students who do not bike is 1 : 4. In Mr. Patel's class, 1 out of every 4 students bikes to school. Which class has the greater fraction of bikers?
options: Ms. Chen's class, because 1 : 4 means 1 out of every 4 students bikes, and that is the bigger share.
They are the same, because both classes use the numbers 1 and 4, so 1 : 4 and 1 out of 4 match.
You cannot tell without knowing how many students are in each class; a bigger class has more bikers.
Mr. Patel's class, because 1/4 of his class bikes but only 1/5 of Ms. Chen's class bikes.
questions.explain: Ms. Chen's 1 : 4 is part-to-part, so her whole is 1 + 4 = 5 parts and 1/5 of her class bikes, while Mr. Patel's 1 out of 4 is already part-to-whole, or 1/4 — and 1/4 is greater than 1/5. The trap is reading 1 : 4 as “1 out of 4”, which mixes up a part-to-part ratio with a part-to-whole one.
